evidence_quotes.quote: To understand how, and under what circumstances community participation in water and sanitation interventions impacts the availability of safe water and sanitation, a change in health status or behaviour and the longevity of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) resources and services.

In the context of this paper, community participation is defined as community members having a role in planning, design, construction, decision-making, delivery or management (including financial, operations and maintenance) of WASH interventions.

We identified five mechanisms that explained the availability, change and longevity outcomes: (1) accountability (policies and procedures to hold communities responsible for their actions and outcomes of an intervention), (2) diffusion (spread of an idea or behaviour by innovators over time through communication among members of a community), (3) market (the interplay between demand and supply of a WASH service or resource), (4) ownership (a sense of possession and control of the WASH service or resource) and (5) shame (a feeling of disgust in one’s behaviour or actions).
This review involved a thorough detailed search, which identified 73 papers, from 29 countries for inclusion.

This involved reading and rereading the papers, first to gain familiarity with the studies, and second to identify outcomes that occur because of community WASH interventions, for example, how community engagement in water and sanitation interventions impact the availability (of safe water and sanitation), a change (in health status or behaviour) and the longevity (of WASH resources).

criterion_notes.c1: Yes. Examines availability of safe water and sanitation facilities/services and longevity of water and sanitation infrastructure and services at the individual, household, and community levels in LMICs.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading diverge (plain = yes; narrow = no). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, community participation in WASH management, water/WASH committees, and local community governance/accountability arrangements qualify as institutional or governance factors (plain_criterion2_decision = include). Under the active 2026-10-13 clarification, however, Criterion 2 requires a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) rather than generic project delivery or behavioural promotion. Here, the focal exposure is community participation in WASH project delivery, hardware operations and maintenance, and behavioural promotion (e.g. CLTS, shame, peer diffusion, psychological ownership). Brief mentions of community fines for open defecation (behaviour change) or willingness to pay user fees for rural O&M are descriptive contextual elements within a generic participatory project-delivery and behaviour-change synthesis rather than an analysis of a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule governing service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Systematic realist review (following RAMESES standards) synthesising 73 peer-reviewed primary empirical studies from 29 LMICs published between 2010 and 2020.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes. Synthesises two access-relevant outcome categories alongside health/behaviour change: (1) availability of clean water and sanitation resources/services at the individual or community level, and (3) longevity and ongoing functionality/maintenance of water and sanitation infrastructure and services.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population (communities and households in 29 LMICs across 73 primary studies), exposure (community participation in planning, design, construction, decision-making, delivery, or management of WASH interventions), outcomes (WASH service/resource availability, health/behaviour change, and infrastructure/service longevity), and study design (realist review) are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Realist review (systematic realist synthesis of 73 primary empirical studies)
country: 29 low-income and middle-income countries (synthesised across 73 studies; individual countries shown in Figure 2 and online supplemental appendix)
population_and_sample: Communities and households in 29 low-income and middle-income countries across 73 primary empirical studies (2010-2020)
exposure: Community participation in planning, design, construction, decision-making, delivery, or management of WASH hardware and behavioural-promotion interventions
outcome: Availability of safe water and sanitation facilities/services, hygiene/sanitation behaviour and health status changes, and longevity of WASH infrastructure and services
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While this realist review of 73 LMIC studies examines water and sanitation availability and service longevity (c1, c3, c4, c5, c6 met) and would qualify under the literal plain wording of Criterion 2 via community governance/committee participation (plain_criterion2_decision = include), its exposure is generic participatory WASH project delivery, community hardware O&M, and behavioural promotion (CLTS, shame, peer diffusion, psychological ownership) rather than a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access.
